title: Indian Pilots Urge Government to Suspend All UAE Flights Amid Gulf Crisis
excerpt: The Airline Pilots' Association of India has demanded the DGCA halt commercial flights to the UAE and other high-risk Gulf airspace, calling continued operations 'wilful endangerment' as EASA warns of missile and drone threats through July 29.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • ALPA demands suspension of Indian flights to UAE due to escalating military threats in the region.
  • EASA warns against flying over UAE and Gulf states until at least July 29 due to conflict risks.
  • Over 20 international airlines have suspended services to Dubai and Abu Dhabi through October 2026.
  • India's maritime regulator halted deployment of seafarers through the Strait of Hormuz after recent attacks.
  • The Airline Pilots' Association of India (ALPA) has demanded the DGCA suspend all Indian commercial flights to the UAE and other high-risk Gulf airspace, warning that airlines lack the intelligence capability to assess threats in active war zones.
  • EASA issued a Conflict Zone Information Bulletin on July 14 advising operators to avoid airspace over the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar and the Gulf of Oman until at least July 29.
  • India's maritime regulator barred deployment of Indian seafarers through the Strait of Hormuz after two sailors were killed, with over 15,000 still stranded in the Gulf.
  • More than 20 international airlines have suspended Dubai and Abu Dhabi services through October 2026, while Indian carriers continue operating Gulf routes.

India's largest pilot body has intensified pressure on aviation authorities to halt commercial flights to the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf states, arguing that the worsening US-Iran conflict has made the region's airspace fundamentally unsafe for civilian aircraft.

The Airline Pilots' Association of India (ALPA) wrote to the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) demanding an immediate suspension of operations into high-risk conflict zones in West Asia. The association warned that continued flights into the region amounted to "wilful endangerment of human life."

"Operating flights into, or in close proximity to, an active war zone constitutes a serious and unacceptable risk to the safety of passengers, flight crew, and aircraft."

— Airline Pilots' Association of India, in its letter to the DGCA

Gulf Airspace Under Siege

ALPA's demands carry new urgency as the Gulf's aviation infrastructure buckles under escalating military confrontation. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) issued Conflict Zone Information Bulletin CZIB-2026-07 on July 14, classifying airspace above the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar and parts of the Gulf of Oman as high-risk. The bulletin identified missile launches, drone activity, military interceptions, falling debris and possible aircraft misidentification as major hazards.

"ALPA also flagged the unresolved issue of war-risk insurance, noting pilots have received "no documentary evidence or formal assurance" that their coverage remains valid in active conflict zones."

"ALPA also flagged the unresolved issue of war-risk insurance, noting pilots have received "no documentary evidence or formal assurance" that their coverage remains valid in active conflict zones."

On July 18, Kuwait temporarily suspended all operations at Kuwait International Airport after its armed forces intercepted hostile aerial targets. That day saw 170 flight cancellations and 829 delays across the region, with Dubai International recording 291 disrupted flights. Emirates alone saw 197 services delayed, according to tracking data. Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed responsibility for cruise missile attacks on two Emirati oil supertankers — a significant escalation from earlier drone strikes.

Pilots Challenge India's Regulatory Response

ALPA sharply criticised the DGCA's March 19 safety advisory, which directed individual airlines to conduct their own risk assessments. The association argued that "commercial airlines do not possess the requisite intelligence, surveillance capabilities, or geopolitical risk assessment infrastructure" for such evaluations, calling the approach dangerously inadequate.

The letter cited past tragedies where civilian aircraft were shot down during conflicts: Iran Air Flight 655 by the United States, Libyan Arab Airlines Flight 114 by Israel, and Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752 by Iran. ALPA also flagged the unresolved issue of war-risk insurance, noting pilots have received "no documentary evidence or formal assurance" that their coverage remains valid in active conflict zones. The association called for an inquiry into Air India's decision-making on Gulf operations.

The gap between Indian and foreign carrier responses has widened sharply. Air India Express launched new Navi Mumbai-Abu Dhabi and Indore-Abu Dhabi services on July 15 — even as EASA's conflict bulletin was freshly in effect. Meanwhile, over 20 foreign carriers have suspended Gulf services. British Airways paused Dubai operations until October 25. Lufthansa extended suspensions until September 13, while Singapore Airlines, Air Canada and Cathay Pacific cancelled Dubai flights deep into autumn.

UAE-based carriers — Emirates, Etihad, Flydubai and Air Arabia — continue operating under their national regulators' risk assessments, though both Emirates and Etihad have issued urgent advisories urging passengers to monitor flight status closely.

Crisis Extends to the Seas

India's Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) on July 16 ordered companies to stop deploying Indian seafarers on vessels through the Strait of Hormuz "until further orders," according to Reuters. Two Indian sailors had been killed in attacks on merchant vessels in the preceding days. More than 15,000 Indian seafarers remain stranded west of the strait, with nine Indian-linked vessels carrying approximately 198 crew unable to transit.

"We can stop the new sets of crews from joining in those areas. But what about those thousands of seafarers who are still trapped in those deadly seas?"

— Manoj Yadav, General Secretary, Forward Seamen's Union of India, to Reuters

New Delhi summoned Iran's deputy ambassador to protest the seafarer deaths.

What Comes Next

The US, Canada and Australia updated their Middle East travel advisories on July 17, classifying Gulf nations under Level 3 parameters. EASA's bulletin expires July 29, but further escalation could trigger extensions. For the estimated 3.5 million Indian nationals in the UAE, ALPA's unanswered demand for a centralised risk assessment leaves India's commercial fleet operating in what its own pilots call unacceptable safety grey areas.
